\begin{abstract}
Crowd crushes are driven by local density, yet most camera analytics report only a head count per image. CrowdSafe converts fixed CCTV video into crowd density in \pmsq{} per floor zone, forecasts it 10--60\,s ahead and raises tiered alerts, using only pretrained models. A zero-shot CLIP-EBC density map is projected onto the floor through a camera model fitted to furniture of known size; RAFT optical flow adds motion features; Chronos-2 forecasts each zone zero-shot, and split conformal calibration sets its 90\,\% upper bound. On our classroom CCTV (four cameras, three rooms, 6,715 labelled heads) CLIP-EBC counts with a mean absolute error of 2.0--5.1 people per frame and zone density is within 0.08--0.10\,\pmsq{} of the labels; a learned detector--density fusion fails on unseen rooms. On held-out runs the calibrated Chronos-2 bound holds for 84--96\,\% of forecasts, against 66--85\,\% for persistence on real J\"ulich crowds. Because our CCTV never becomes dangerous, alerts are evaluated on J\"ulich experiments and JuPedSim simulations: alerts on current density never warn before a zone reaches 4\,\pmsq, while forecast-driven alerts warn in time for 34\,\% of 47 simulated events (median 7.5\,s ahead) and one of nine real events. The pipeline runs live on one A100 GPU with 0.49\,s median latency. Warnings come seconds, not minutes, ahead.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
crowd counting, crowd density estimation, zero-shot learning, time-series forecasting, conformal prediction, optical flow, early warning
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Background}
Crowd disasters are caused by local density, not by the total number of people present. Dangerous conditions begin at roughly 4--5\,\pmsq, with stop-and-go and turbulent flow at higher densities~\cite{fruin1971,helbing2007}. Many venues already have fixed CCTV cameras.

\subsection{Motivation}
Crowd-counting methods and most deployed analytics report people per image~\cite{zhang2016mcnn,li2018csrnet,ma2025clipebc}. Such a count does not show \emph{where} density builds up and cannot be compared with density limits without knowing the floor area each image region covers, which requires a camera calibration that existing installations rarely have. Anticipating danger also needs a forecaster that works without venue-specific training data, because dangerous events are rare.

\subsection{Problem Statement}
Given an existing CCTV camera and a few measured dimensions in the scene, estimate the density of each floor zone every second, forecast it with a reliable upper bound, and raise an alert \emph{before} a zone becomes dangerous, with few false alarms.

\subsection{Objectives}
(i) Zone density in \pmsq{} without training a counting model; (ii) a forecast bound whose coverage is checked on held-out data; (iii) alert lead time and false alarms measured on real and simulated dangerous crowds; (iv) live latency on one GPU.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A camera calibration from desk tops and straight edges, validated against measured distances not used in the fit.
\item A held-out counting evaluation on real CCTV, including the negative result that learned detector--density fusion does not transfer across rooms.
\item Zero-shot, conformally calibrated forecasting of zone density.
\item A strict early-warning evaluation showing that forecast-driven alerts warn only seconds ahead.
\item A live implementation with measured latency and a replay dashboard.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Crowd Counting: Detection versus Density Estimation}
Density-map methods estimate a per-pixel density whose sum is the count: MCNN introduced ShanghaiTech~\cite{zhang2016mcnn}, CSRNet used dilated convolutions~\cite{li2018csrnet}, and CLIP-EBC recasts counting as blockwise classification on CLIP, trained on NWPU-Crowd~\cite{ma2025clipebc,wang2021nwpu}. Detectors such as YOLO11~\cite{yolo11}, including CrowdHuman-trained models~\cite{shao2018crowdhuman}, count only visible people.

\subsection{Crowd Dynamics and Precursors of Crowd Disasters}
Helbing et al.\ described the transition from laminar to stop-and-go to turbulent flow before the 2006 Hajj disaster and proposed crowd pressure, density times velocity variance, as a danger indicator~\cite{helbing2007}. The J\"ulich archive provides trajectories of controlled high-density experiments~\cite{julich_archive}; PedPy~\cite{pedpy} analyses and JuPedSim~\cite{jupedsim} simulates such data.

\subsection{Crowd Density and Flow Forecasting}
ST-ResNet forecasts the inflow and outflow of city regions~\cite{zhang2017stresnet}, and Niu et al.\ forecast future crowd distributions from video~\cite{niu2020overcrowdedness}. Chronos~\cite{ansari2024chronos} and Chronos-2~\cite{ansari2025chronos2} forecast new series without training. Split conformal prediction gives a bound with finite-sample coverage~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}.

\subsection{Integrated Crowd Monitoring and Early-Warning Systems}
Cao and Huang estimate and predict crowd density over a multi-camera network~\cite{cao2013video}; Niu et al.\ motivate their forecaster with over-crowding alerts~\cite{niu2020overcrowdedness}.

\subsection{Research Gap}
Table~\ref{tab:gap} summarises these studies. In the sources reviewed we found no evaluation that combines metric zone density from an uncalibrated existing camera, a forecast bound with verified coverage, and alert lead time measured with an explicit protocol on real dangerous crowds. CrowdSafe studies this combination with pretrained components only; we do not claim the cited systems cannot do so.

\section{Proposed Methodology}
\label{sec:method}
CrowdSafe is a chain of steps that turns camera frames into alerts, and each step works on what the previous one produced (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}). A camera model, fitted once, tells the system how image pixels relate to the floor. Every second, a frame is turned into a map of where people are and a pair of frames into a field of how they move; both are collected per floor zone into densities in \pmsq{} and motion statistics, stored as one row per zone and second. Every 5\,s, each zone's recent rows are forecast, the forecast's calibrated upper bound is turned into a risk level, and sustained high levels become alerts on a dashboard. Below, each step is described in general terms, followed by how we applied it to our classroom, J\"ulich and simulation data.

\subsection{Camera Calibration}
To speak of density in \pmsq, the system must know which floor area each part of the image shows. CrowdSafe fits a camera model, a pinhole camera with radial lens distortion ($k_1,k_2$), focal length, position and tilt, by robust least squares to a few objects of known size in a still frame and to straight edges, which must look straight once the distortion is removed. A tape measure is the only extra resource. Once fitted, the model can carry any pixel to a point on the floor at a chosen height, which is what the zone and motion steps rely on.
In classrooms H705 and H706 we used desk tops of measured length (1.00\,m) as rectangles, leaving each desk's position free so that the row and column spacing could later serve as independent checks, and door frames and the ceiling duct as straight edges. In the computer lab H103, monitors hide most desk tops, so long table edges at measured positions, vertical edges and the measured camera height were used instead.

\subsection{Zone Definition and Area Computation}
The floor is then divided into zones on a plan in metres, small enough that a dangerous pocket is not averaged away by an empty corner. Using the camera model, each zone is projected into the image at the height where heads appear, which gives the image region $M_z$ that belongs to zone $z$ and the floor area $A_z$ that the camera actually sees. These two quantities are what later turn a count of people into a density.
In each classroom we used 3$\times$3 seating blocks plus the front aisle (4--16\,m$^2$ each), projected at seated head height (1.2\,m); in H103 a glass partition that shows the neighbouring room was masked out.

\subsection{People Counting}
Every second, a frame of the video is passed to a pretrained density model, CLIP-EBC ViT-B/16 with NWPU-Crowd weights~\cite{ma2025clipebc,wang2021nwpu}, used without any training. Applied in non-overlapping 224-pixel windows (45 windows for a zero-padded 1080p frame), it returns a density map $D_t$ of 135$\times$240 cells, one per 8$\times$8 pixels, whose values are expected numbers of heads, so it can be summed over any region of the image. Person detectors instead return boxes; YOLO11l~\cite{yolo11} and a YOLO11 head detector trained on CrowdHuman~\cite{shao2018crowdhuman} therefore serve as baselines. Because detectors can be more accurate when only a few people are present, we also test combining their frame counts with the density model: a hard switch to the detector below a threshold $\tau$, a constant or 50/50 weighting, and a learned per-frame weight. These combinations act on whole-frame counts and are compared at frame level, while the zone pipeline continues with the density map.
In our recordings, one frame per second of every classroom and lab video was passed through CLIP-EBC; the detectors and combinations were run on the 160 hand-labelled frames to choose the counting route (Section~\ref{sec:count}).

\subsection{Zone Density Estimation in Persons per \texorpdfstring{m$^2$}{m2}}
The density map from the counting step and the zone regions and areas from the zone step meet here. Summing the map inside a zone's region gives its count $c_{z,t}=\sum D_t\odot M_z$, and dividing by the visible area gives its density $\rho_{z,t}=c_{z,t}/A_z$ in \pmsq. Zones with less than 2\,m$^2$ in view are skipped, because their density would be unstable. This per-second density is what the rest of the pipeline watches.
For H705 this produces ten densities every second, one for each seating block and the aisle.

\subsection{Crowd Motion Feature Extraction}
Density shows how full a zone is; motion shows how its crowd is behaving. The same sampled frame and a second frame 0.2\,s later are passed to pretrained RAFT-large optical flow~\cite{teed2020raft} at 544$\times$960 pixels with 12 refinement iterations, and the flow is averaged into the same 135$\times$240 cells as $D_t$. Each displacement is carried to the floor by the camera model, turning pixel shifts into velocities in m/s, and weighted by the density map so that empty floor contributes nothing. Per zone this gives the mean speed, the velocity variance, crowd pressure $\rho\cdot\mathrm{var}$~\cite{helbing2007}, the entropy of an 8-bin direction histogram and the share of counter-flow. The number of people crossing a zone's boundary per second (inflow and outflow) needs individual trajectories, so it is available only where trajectories exist.
For the classroom recordings all motion values come from RAFT and inflow and outflow remain empty; for J\"ulich and simulated runs, speeds and boundary crossings come directly from each person's trajectory.

\subsection{Zone Feature Table Construction}
All measurements now meet in a single table with one row per camera (or run), zone and second, holding count, density, the motion values, inflow, outflow and the data source. Forecasting and alerting read only this table, so any source that can fill it is evaluated in exactly the same way.
Our classroom CCTV fills the table through the density and motion steps. J\"ulich trajectories and JuPedSim simulations fill it directly, using 2\,m$\times$2\,m floor cells as zones; our J\"ulich densities agree exactly with those of PedPy~\cite{pedpy} on six checked runs. This is how dangerous densities, which our classrooms never reached, are passed through the same downstream steps.

\subsection{Crowd Density Forecasting}
Every 5\,s, the last 30\,s of each zone are read from the table as a regular 1-Hz series and forecast 10, 30 and 60\,s ahead. The forecaster is Chronos-2~\cite{ansari2025chronos2}, a pretrained time-series model used zero-shot, either \emph{per zone}, with pressure, inflow, outflow and mean speed as additional inputs (set to zero when missing), or \emph{jointly} over all zones of one camera so that neighbouring zones inform each other. It returns the 10, 50 and 90\,\% quantiles for each zone and horizon. Two simple forecasters serve as baselines: \emph{persistence}, which repeats the last value, and a \emph{physics} fill-rate model, $\rho+(q_{\mathrm{in}}-q_{\mathrm{out}})\,h/A_z$, which needs inflow and outflow. In live operation, a second skipped by a slow cycle is filled with the previous value so that the series stays regular. The horizon limits how early a warning can come, but it is not the warning time itself.
Because most J\"ulich runs last only 1--3\,min, we used 10--60\,s horizons there and on CCTV and added 120\,s on the longer simulations; the physics model could be run only on J\"ulich and simulated data.

\subsection{Reliable Upper Bound via Conformal Calibration}
A forecaster's 90\,\% quantile is not guaranteed to be exceeded only 10\,\% of the time, and point forecasts have no spread at all. CrowdSafe therefore calibrates the upper bound with split conformal prediction~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}: on validation runs it measures how far the realised density rose above the 90\,\% quantile and takes the finite-sample 90\,\% quantile of these residuals as an offset $q_h$ for each horizon. New forecasts then carry the bound $U_{z,h}=\max(0,\,\mathrm{p90}_{z,h}+q_h)$, the worst case the risk step works with.
We fitted the offsets on the validation cameras (cam01, cam03), 39 J\"ulich validation runs and four validation scenarios, and applied them only to the test data. On CCTV the Chronos-2 offsets were tiny (0.001--0.02\,\pmsq), whereas for persistence the offset of 0.14--0.18\,\pmsq{} forms the whole bound.

\subsection{Risk Classification (Low, Medium, High, Critical)}
The calibrated bounds over all horizons and the current density are combined into a worst case, $W_z=\max(\max_h U_{z,h},\,\rho_z)$, which is mapped to Low ($<2$), Medium (2--4), High (4--5) or Critical ($\geq 5$\,\pmsq). The first horizon whose bound reaches 5\,\pmsq{} is reported as the time to critical. Before the first forecast of a run, only the current density is used.
On the H705 recording, for example, a zone at 1.6\,\pmsq{} is shown as Medium because its forecast bound exceeds 2\,\pmsq{} (Fig.~\ref{fig:dashboard}).

\subsection{Precursor-Based Risk Escalation}
The motion values from the feature table can raise a zone's level by one step when they signal trouble: high pressure, direction entropy or counter-flow, low speed, rising density with falling speed (flow collapse), or a fast rise in density. Each signal is kept only if, on validation data, it predicts that a zone at 2--4\,\pmsq{} will reach 4\,\pmsq{} within 60\,s at least twice as often as chance.
We tuned these thresholds on the pooled J\"ulich and simulation validation runs; none passed (Section~\ref{sec:negative}), so the final system raises levels from the forecast bound alone.

\subsection{Alert Generation}
Levels change every 5\,s and can flicker, so an alert manager adds hysteresis: an alert is raised when a zone stays High or above for 10\,s and cleared once it has stayed below High for 30\,s. Each alert records its zone, the highest level reached, the time to critical and a short reason, such as ``forecast upper bound 4.2 \pmsq{} (now 1.8)''.
In the held-out J\"ulich corridor run of Fig.~\ref{fig:timeline}, the bound of zone c3\_2 crossed 4\,\pmsq{} and an alert was raised at 219\,s, 49\,s before the zone itself reached 4\,\pmsq.

\subsection{Dashboard Visualisation}
Finally, the zones, levels, forecasts and alerts are shown to an operator. A FastAPI/WebSocket server replays a stored run by re-running the risk and alert steps on its feature rows and forecasts, and streams one message per second to a Next.js dashboard: the camera video with zones coloured by level and labelled with density, the forecast of a selected zone and the alert feed. The live pipeline (Section~\ref{sec:runtime}) runs the same steps directly on a camera stream.
Fig.~\ref{fig:dashboard} shows the dashboard replaying the H705 recording.

\subsection{Own CCTV Recordings and Annotation}
Two views of classroom H705, classroom H706 and computer lab H103 were recorded with permission (2.6\,h, 1080p). Head points on 160 frames were annotated by correcting model pre-labels. The busiest zone reached 3.2\,\pmsq, so the recordings contain no dangerous density. No faces or identities are stored.

\subsection{ShanghaiTech Benchmark}
ShanghaiTech A and B~\cite{zhang2016mcnn} are standard counting benchmarks~\cite{li2018csrnet}; we use their test sets only to check the zero-shot models.

\subsection{J\"ulich Pedestrian Experiments}
The test experiments, a unidirectional corridor~\cite{julich_uni2013} used by Cao et al.~\cite{cao2017fundamental} and an entrance crowd~\cite{julich_semicircle} used by Sieben et al.~\cite{sieben2017collective}, reach 5.3 and 9.0\,\pmsq.

\subsection{JuPedSim Simulated Scenarios}
Sixteen scenarios in four layouts (classroom, corridor bottleneck, two-exit hall, bidirectional corridor) include arrival surges and exit closures. Desired speeds are $\mathcal{N}(1.34, 0.26^2)$\,m/s~\cite{weidmann1993}. Simulations follow model rules, not real behaviour.

\subsection{Train, Validation, and Test Splits}
No model is trained. Fusion parameters are fitted leave-one-room-out. Conformal offsets use validation cameras, experiments or scenarios and are applied to disjoint test ones; precursor thresholds use the pooled J\"ulich and simulation validation splits. Test data are used for no fitting.

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics}
Counting: MAE in people per frame. Zone density: MAE in \pmsq. Forecasts: MAE and \emph{coverage}, the share of test forecasts at or below the bound (target 0.90). Alerts: an \emph{event} is the first second a zone reaches 4 (or 5)\,\pmsq{} after monitoring starts; it is \emph{warned in time} if an alert was raised at most (longest horizon + 10\,s) before it and more than 15\,s after monitoring began. Lead time is alert-to-event time; a \emph{false alarm} has no event within 120\,s, counted per zone-hour.

\subsection{Hardware and Software}
Density maps, flow, Chronos-2 and latency ran on one shared NVIDIA A100 (40\,GB); label-based counting used ONNX models on a CPU. Simulations used JuPedSim 1.4.2 and analysis PedPy 1.5.1. No model is trained; the deployed path has about 222\,M parameters (Table~\ref{tab:models}), extracting features from all 2.6\,h of CCTV took 33.5\,min on the A100, and the 16 simulations took 9.7\,min on a CPU.

\section{Results and Discussion}

\subsection{Counting Accuracy on ShanghaiTech}
Zero-shot CLIP-EBC reaches an MAE of 66.95 (A) and 11.66 (B), close to CSRNet trained on ShanghaiTech (Table~\ref{tab:counting}); detectors miss most people in these dense images.

\subsection{Counting Accuracy on CCTV and Fusion Ablation}
\label{sec:count}
CLIP-EBC is most accurate in every room. Detectors undercount by 6--17 people per frame because desks, students and monitors hide bodies; they are better only in near-empty frames (below 20 people in H705: 0.86 vs 1.15). Within one room, fusion looked strong (constant weight 1.59, learned 2.09, CLIP-EBC 5.30), but leave-one-room-out reverses this (Table~\ref{tab:fusion}).

\subsection{Calibration Accuracy}
Reprojection errors are 3.6--4.2\,px. On distances not used in the fit, H705 row spacing is 0.99 vs 0.96\,m measured (+3\,\%) and mean desk spacing $-5$\,\%; an H706 door is 1.23 vs 1.12\,m (+10\,\%); lab table edges lie within 0.03--0.18\,m. We treat calibration as accurate to about $\pm 5$\,\%.

\subsection{Zone Density Accuracy}
Zone-density MAE is 0.101 (H705), 0.081 (H706) and 0.078\,\pmsq{} (H103), with 94--98\,\% of heads inside a zone; changing the head height from 1.1 to 1.6\,m alters it by at most 0.03. These errors are small next to the 2\,\pmsq{} band width but were measured only up to 1.67\,\pmsq.

\subsection{Forecasting Accuracy and Upper-Bound Reliability}
\label{sec:forecast}
Chronos-2 matches persistence on average error (Table~\ref{tab:forecast}) and its calibrated bound holds near 90\,\% on all sources, while persistence drops to 0.66 on J\"ulich at 30\,s. Where the true density is at least 4\,\pmsq, every bound under-covers, but Chronos-2 keeps 0.76--0.88 on J\"ulich against 0.56--0.78 for persistence. Our CCTV test cameras never reach 2\,\pmsq.

\subsection{Early-Warning Performance}
Alerts on current density never warn before a zone reaches 4\,\pmsq{} (Table~\ref{tab:alerts}). Forecast-driven alerts warn in time for about a third of 47 simulated events, with median leads of 7.5\,s (Chronos-2) and 25\,s (physics, more false alarms), and for one of nine J\"ulich events. Fig.~\ref{fig:timeline} shows the J\"ulich run with the Chronos-2 success: zone c3\_2 was warned 49\,s ahead, while earlier alerts in other zones fall outside the protocol window. For a 5\,\pmsq{} event, an alert at 4\,\pmsq{} is itself an early warning, and current-density alerts warn for 38\,\% of 34 simulated events. Our CCTV produced no events and no false alarms in 8.6 zone-hours. Zones fill from safe to 4\,\pmsq{} in about 10--20\,s, which explains the short leads: the forecast horizon is not the warning time.

\subsection{Runtime Performance}
\label{sec:runtime}
On one shared A100 with cam02 played at real speed, the live pipeline has a median latency of 0.49\,s (p95 1.6\,s) from frame to alert state, with 94\,\% of 1-s cycles on time and 2.0\,GB of GPU memory; median stage times are 159\,ms (CLIP-EBC), 103\,ms (RAFT) and 54\,ms (Chronos-2, every 5\,s). Unpaced, 908\,s of video took 196\,s (4.6$\times$ real time). A laptop CPU needs about 19\,s per second of video. Table~\ref{tab:models} lists the size, input, output and time of each model.

\subsection{Comparison with Existing Systems}
On ShanghaiTech A, zero-shot CLIP-EBC is close to CSRNet and better than MCNN, both trained on that dataset (Table~\ref{tab:counting}); training regimes differ, so this is not a claim of superiority. System-level studies~\cite{cao2013video,niu2020overcrowdedness} use different data and metrics and cannot be compared numerically.

\subsection{Negative Findings}
\label{sec:negative}
\emph{Learned fusion} looked best within one room only because detector and density errors cancelled there; on unseen rooms it is the worst combination (Table~\ref{tab:fusion}). \emph{Motion precursors:} on J\"ulich validation alone, slowing (precision 0.54, 3.8$\times$ the base rate) and direction entropy (2.0$\times$) passed, but pooled with simulation none did, so none is used. Variants of alert timing (shorter hold, rate of rise, shorter history) each helped one forecaster and hurt another, so the default was kept. A looser early scoring, which credited alerts raised at the start of monitoring, had reported 56\,\% and 86\,\% warned; we report only the strict values.

\subsection{Limitations}
Calibration is approximate and assumes seated head height. Our CCTV has no dangerous densities, so danger-level results rest on nine real J\"ulich events and on simulation. CCTV speeds are not validated against ground truth, and inflow/outflow are not measured from CCTV. Latency was measured for one camera on a shared GPU.

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}

\subsection{Conclusion}
Pretrained, zero-shot components turn existing CCTV into zone density with errors around 0.1\,\pmsq{} and run live on one GPU in under a second. A conformally calibrated zero-shot forecaster gives a bound that holds near its target and degrades less than persistence at high density. Forecast-driven alerts warn for about a third of simulated dangerous events and one of nine real ones, seconds rather than minutes ahead.

\subsection{Future Work}
Longer warnings need information beyond one view: entrance cameras, gate counters, schedules and inflow measured across zone boundaries from CCTV. Further steps are validating CCTV speeds, recording staged crowding with a calibrated camera, density-conditional calibration and multi-camera latency tests.
